title: Habit remnants may remain, but justifying acts and peace cease in mortal falls—not in lighter slips
source_text: LII. Ac praeterea quamvis reliquias habituum istorum manere doceat etiam in iis qui gravissime peccant, monet tamen eorum praecipuos actus & operationes in illis cessare, atque intercidere. Nec enim in eo statu, fidei justificantis, & fiduciae ac spei de propria salute, & remissione peccatorum suorum, actus ab iis exerceri posse, & spiritualem consolationem ac pacem retineri. Nihil vero tale renatis accidit, quum in peccata leviora ex infirmitate labuntur: Nec enim ejusmodi peccata impediunt, quominus fides & spes, sanctaque illa fiducia, quam Spiritus Sanctus nobis ingenerat, solitos actus in iis exerceant: sed cum talibus peccatis simul in iis manent misericordia divinae fiducia, & salutis certa spes, ac remissionis peccatorum suorum sensus ac per-suasio.
pass_a_gloss: And further, although he teaches that remnants of those habits remain even in those who sin most gravely, yet he warns that their principal acts and operations cease and are cut off in them. For in that state acts of justifying faith, and of confidence and hope concerning one’s own salvation and the remission of one’s sins, cannot be exercised by them, nor spiritual consolation and peace retained. But nothing of the sort befalls the regenerate when they fall into lighter sins from infirmity: for sins of that sort do not hinder faith and hope and that holy confidence which the Holy Spirit begets in us from exercising their wonted acts in them; but together with such sins there remain in them confidence of divine mercy, and sure hope of salvation, and the sense and persuasion of the remission of their sins.
pass_b_english: Even if habit-remnants linger after capital falls, justifying acts, peace, and consolation stop.
Infirmity’s lighter slips leave faith, hope, and Spirit-wrought confidence still acting with mercy-trust and pardon-sense.

choices.why: Principal acts cease in mortal state.
